extraction.name: LAMBADA
extraction.description: A dataset to evaluate computational models for text understanding via a word prediction task where the last word is guessable by humans from the whole passage but not from the last sentence alone.
extraction.creator: Denis Paperno, German Kruszewski, Angeliki Lazaridou, Quan Ngoc Pham, Raffaella Bernardi, Sandro Pezzelle, Marco Baroni, Gemma Boleda, Raquel Fernandez
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Passages were sourced from the Book Corpus, filtered automatically using language models, then evaluated by human subjects in a three-step CrowdFlower pipeline; passages were included only if two subjects guessed the target word from the whole passage and no subject could guess it from the target sentence alone.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Unpublished novels from the Book Corpus after duplicate removal and filtering of potentially offensive material.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The source corpus underwent duplicate removal and offensive-material filtering; novels were split into training and development+testing partitions; passages easy for standard language models were excluded using a probability threshold.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human subjects on CrowdFlower guessed target words in three steps: one subject guessed from the whole passage, then a second subject guessed from the whole passage, then additional subjects guessed from the target sentence only until the word was guessed or 10 unsuccessful guesses were reached; passages were kept only if both whole-passage guesses were correct and no sentence-only subject guessed the word.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper reports discard rates across annotation steps and explains that step 2 was added after a pilot study because step 1 alone did not ensure passages were easy given discourse context; the authors also enforced that the same subject could not judge the same item in both passage and sentence conditions.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: At least 12 human judgments for included items: 1 in step 1, 1 in step 2, and up to 10 unsuccessful sentence-only judgments in step 3.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Proper nouns are heavily overrepresented in LAMBADA, and direct speech appears more often than in the input items overall.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset construction uses very strict inclusion criteria and a strict hit-or-miss approach, which excludes plausible synonymous continuations; the authors also note that standard language models are bound to fail on it by design because early filters selected passages where simple language models failed.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: A benchmark and challenging test set for evaluating language models on broad-context understanding; the development set can be used to fine-tune models, while models should be trained on raw text from the training partition.

name.evidence: In this paper, we introduce the LAMBADA dataset (LAnguage Modeling Broadened to Account for Discourse Aspects).

description.evidence: We introduce LAMBADA, a dataset to evaluate the capabilities of computational models for text understanding by means of a word prediction task.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: The LAMBADA data come from the Book Corpus (Zhu et al., 2015). To reduce time and cost of dataset collection, we filtered out passages that are relatively easy for standard language models. A random sample of the remaining passages were then evaluated by human subjects through the CrowdFlower crowdsourcing service in three steps.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: The LAMBADA data come from the Book Corpus (Zhu et al., 2015). The corpus, after duplicate removal and filtering out of potentially offensive material with a stop word list, contains 5,325 novels and 465 million words.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: The corpus, after duplicate removal and filtering out of potentially offensive material with a stop word list, contains 5,325 novels and 465 million words. We randomly divided the novels into equally-sized training and development+testing partitions. Any passage whose target word had probability ≥0.00175 according to any of the language models was excluded.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: A random sample of the remaining passages were then evaluated by human subjects through the CrowdFlower crowdsourcing service in three steps. For a given passage, 1. one human subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage (comprising the context and the target sentence); if the guess was right, 2. a second subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage; if that guess was also right, 3. more subjects tried to guess the target word based on the target sentence only, until the word was guessed or the number of unsuccessful guesses reached 10; if no subject was able to guess the target word, the passage was added to the LAMBADA dataset.

rai:dataAnnotationPlatform.evidence: A random sample of the remaining passages were then evaluated by human subjects through the CrowdFlower crowdsourcing service in three steps.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: Step 2 was added based on a pilot study that revealed that, while step 3 was enough to ensure that the data could not be guessed with the local context only, step 1 alone did not ensure that the data were easy given the discourse context. We made sure that it was not possible for the same subject to judge the same item in both passage and sentence conditions (details in SM).

rai:annotationsPerItem.evidence: We required two consecutive subjects to exactly match the missing word, and we made sure that no subject (out of ten) was able to provide it based on local context only, even when given 3 guesses.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: Figure 2(b) shows that most target words in LAMBADA are proper nouns (48%), followed by common nouns (37%) and, at a distance, verbs (7.7%). In fact, proper nouns are hugely overrepresented in LAMBADA, while the other categories are under-represented, compared to the POS distribution in the input. As a final observation, intriguingly, the LAMBADA items contain (quoted) direct speech significantly more often than the input items overall (71% of LAMBADA items vs. 61% of items in the input sample).

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: Note that the criteria for passage inclusion were very strict: We required two consecutive subjects to exactly match the missing word, and we made sure that no subject (out of ten) was able to provide it based on local context only, even when given 3 guesses. We also note that, because of the way we have constructed LAMBADA, standard language models are bound to fail on it by design: one of our first filters (see Section 3.1) was to choose passages where a number of simple language models were failing to predict the upcoming word.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: We thus propose LAMBADA as a challenging test set, meant to encourage the development of new models capable of genuine understanding of broad context in natural language text. The development data can be used to fine-tune models to the specifics of the LAMBADA passages.
